arrows.label: Atomic radius
arrows.cause: Across a period each step adds a proton and an electron to the same shell, and the stronger pull draws that shell in; down a group every period adds a new, larger shell.

exceptions.note: d-block contraction: the ten 3d electrons shield poorly, so gallium is barely larger than aluminium.
Lanthanide contraction: the fourteen 4f electrons shield poorly, so hafnium is almost the size of zirconium.

arrows.label: First ionization energy
arrows.cause: Across a period the outermost electron feels a growing effective nuclear charge in the same shell; down a group it sits in a larger shell, farther out and better shielded.

exceptions.note: Lower than beryllium: boron's outermost electron is in 2p, higher in energy and better shielded than 2s.
Lower than nitrogen: oxygen's fourth 2p electron has to share an orbital, and the pair repels.
Lower than magnesium, for the same reason as boron (3p after 3s).
Lower than phosphorus, for the same reason as oxygen (pairing in 3p).

arrows.label: Electron affinity
arrows.cause: An added electron is held more strongly where the effective nuclear charge is higher and the shell smaller; the pattern is irregular because filled and half-filled subshells resist an extra electron.

exceptions.note: Noble gases: an extra electron would have to start a new shell; no stable negative ion forms.
Nitrogen: the half-filled 2p subshell means the added electron must pair.
Group 2: the filled s subshell means the added electron must enter the higher p subshell.

arrows.label: Electronegativity (Pauling)
arrows.cause: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom in a bond pulls shared electrons towards itself, so it follows the same reasoning about nuclear charge and size as the ionization energy.

arrows.label: Metallic character
arrows.cause: Metals give up electrons easily; that becomes easier as the outermost electrons are held more loosely, towards the lower left of the table.

arrows.label: Nonmetallic character
arrows.cause: The mirror image of metallic character: atoms that hold on to electrons and gain them readily lie towards the upper right.

arrows.label: Effective nuclear charge (valence)
arrows.cause: Each step across adds a proton but only weak shielding from the new electron in the same shell; down a group the extra protons are largely balanced by the added inner shells.

arrows.label: Shielding
arrows.cause: Inner electrons screen the nucleus: across a period their number stays the same, while down a group each new period adds a complete inner shell.

arrows.label: Polarizability
arrows.cause: Larger, more loosely held electron clouds are easier to distort with an electric field, so polarizability follows atomic size.

arrows.label: Ionic radius (same charge)
arrows.cause: For ions of the same charge the reasoning for atoms holds: more nuclear charge pulls the same shell in, and a new shell makes the ion larger.

arrows.label: Reactivity
arrows.cause: Metals react by losing electrons, which gets easier down a group; nonmetals react by gaining electrons, which gets harder down a group.

exceptions.note: Noble gases: filled shells make them largely unreactive.

heatmaps.caption: Boiling point as listed by PubChem (Jefferson Lab).

heatmaps.caption: Density in g/cm³ as listed by PubChem, on a logarithmic scale because gases are about a thousand times less dense than solids.

heatmaps.caption: Standard atomic weight from NIST AWIC; for interval elements, IUPAC's single abridged value (CIAAW). Elements without a standard atomic weight are hatched and say why.

heatmaps.label: Number of stable isotopes
heatmaps.caption: Number of ground-state isotopes that IAEA marks as stable.

heatmaps.label: Longest half-life
heatmaps.caption: Half-life of the longest-lived isotope, for elements without a stable isotope (IAEA), on a logarithmic scale in seconds.

heatmaps.label: 1s electron speed (v/c ≈ Zα)
heatmaps.caption: Hydrogenic estimate of the 1s electron's speed as a fraction of the speed of light, v/c ≈ Zα, with α from CODATA 2022. Computed, not measured; it shows where relativity matters.

maps.label: Blocks
maps.caption: The subshell being filled at each element under the Madelung rule (lutetium and lawrencium in the d-block).

classes.label: s-block
classes.description: The outermost electrons are s electrons.

classes.label: p-block
classes.description: Filling a p subshell.

classes.label: d-block
classes.description: Filling a d subshell.

classes.label: f-block
classes.description: Filling an f subshell.

maps.label: State at room conditions
maps.caption: Standard state as listed by PubChem; elements whose state has only been predicted are shown as unknown.

classes.label: Solid
classes.description: Solid at room temperature and pressure.

classes.label: Liquid
classes.description: Liquid at room temperature and pressure (mercury, bromine).

classes.label: Gas
classes.description: Gas at room temperature and pressure.

classes.label: Unknown
classes.description: Never made in a quantity whose state could be observed.

maps.label: Madelung anomalies
maps.caption: Where NIST's measured ground configuration differs from the Aufbau (Madelung) prediction.

classes.label: Breaks the Aufbau rule
classes.description: The measured configuration differs from the Madelung prediction.

classes.label: Follows the Aufbau rule
classes.description: The measured configuration is the one the rule predicts.

classes.label: Not measured
classes.description: Only a predicted configuration exists (Z ≥ 109).

maps.label: Radioactive or stable
maps.caption: From IAEA LiveChart: elements with at least one stable isotope; radioactive elements that occur naturally enough to have a standard atomic weight (Bi, Th, Pa, U); and the rest.

classes.label: Has stable isotopes
classes.description: At least one isotope is stable.

classes.label: Radioactive, occurs naturally
classes.description: No stable isotope, but natural enough to have a standard atomic weight.

classes.label: Radioactive, no standard weight
classes.description: No stable isotope and no standard atomic weight.

maps.label: Discovery era
maps.caption: Year of discovery as listed by PubChem, grouped into eras.

classes.label: Antiquity
classes.description: Known since antiquity.
From the discovery of phosphorus (1669) to the end of the 18th century.
The 19th century: electrochemistry and spectroscopy.
Radioactivity and the last natural elements.
Reactors and accelerators: the synthetic elements.

classes.label: 2000 on
classes.description: The heaviest elements, made a few atoms at a time.

maps.label: Ground-state hyperfine structure
maps.caption: Whether the ground level of the reference isotope has hyperfine structure, and if not, why (rules in SPEC §5.1).

classes.label: Value compiled
classes.description: The splitting is in the curated table.

classes.label: Exists, not yet compiled
classes.description: Hyperfine structure exists; the value is not yet in our curated table.

classes.label: None: ground level J = 0
classes.description: A J = 0 ground level cannot split.

classes.label: None: nuclear spin I = 0
classes.description: Every naturally occurring isotope has I = 0.

classes.label: No natural isotope
classes.description: No naturally occurring isotope to serve as reference.

maps.label: How IE₁ was obtained
maps.caption: NIST's own markers on the first ionization energy: measured, semi-empirical [ ] or theoretical ( ).

classes.label: Measured
classes.description: Derived from evaluated experimental data.

classes.label: Semi-empirical [ ]
classes.description: Interpolated or extrapolated from known values.

classes.label: Theoretical ( )
classes.description: From an ab-initio calculation.

classes.label: None in NIST
classes.description: NIST lists none; a published prediction is shown, flagged as predicted.

maps.label: Kind of atomic weight
maps.caption: Whether IUPAC gives a single standard atomic weight, an interval reflecting natural variation, or none (NIST AWIC).

classes.label: Single value
classes.description: One value with its uncertainty.

classes.label: Interval
classes.description: Varies in nature; IUPAC gives a range.

classes.label: None
classes.description: No stable isotope: the mass number of the longest-lived isotope is shown.

maps.label: Laser-cooled
maps.caption: Elements whose neutral atoms, singly charged ions or both have been laser-cooled, from the curated table tools/curated/lasercooling.toml (first-cooling papers cited per row).

classes.label: Atoms and ions
classes.description: Both the neutral atom and the singly charged ion have been laser-cooled.

classes.label: Neutral atoms
classes.description: Neutral atoms have been laser-cooled.

classes.label: Ions only
classes.description: Singly charged ions have been laser-cooled; neutral atoms not (yet).

classes.label: Not laser-cooled
classes.description: No laser cooling of this element is in our table.

maps.label: Clock species
maps.caption: Atoms and ions on the BIPM list of recommended standard frequencies, the caesium transition that defines the second, and the thorium-229 nuclear transition.

classes.label: Defines the second
classes.description: The caesium-133 hyperfine frequency is fixed at exactly 9 192 631 770 Hz.

classes.label: Secondary representation
classes.description: A transition of this element is a BIPM secondary representation of the second.

classes.label: Standard or candidate frequency
classes.description: On the BIPM list of recommended frequencies but not a secondary representation, or a nuclear-clock candidate.

classes.label: None
classes.description: No clock or standard frequency of this element is listed.

maps.label: Elements in the SI
maps.caption: Elements that define or realize SI units today (including recommended radiations for the metre), and those that did so only in the past (definitions and prototypes), from the BIPM and the CGPM resolutions.

classes.label: Role in today's SI
classes.description: Defines or realizes an SI unit today.

classes.label: Past role only
classes.description: Was part of a definition or a prototype that has since been replaced.

classes.label: None
classes.description: No role in the definition or realization of SI units.

maps.label: Essential for plants
maps.caption: Elements plants cannot complete their life cycle without, and elements that benefit some plants, from tools/curated/biology.toml (Marschner's Mineral Nutrition of Higher Plants and cited reviews).

classes.label: Essential
classes.description: Required by all higher plants.

classes.label: Beneficial
classes.description: Promotes growth in some plants, or is required by some taxa only.

classes.label: Not essential
classes.description: Not known to be essential or beneficial for plants.

maps.label: Essential for humans
maps.caption: Elements the human body needs, and elements whose need is probable but not proven, from tools/curated/biology.toml (EFSA dietary reference values and cited reviews).

classes.label: Essential
classes.description: A dietary requirement is established.

classes.label: Probably essential
classes.description: Evidence for a requirement exists but is not conclusive.

classes.label: Not essential
classes.description: Not known to be essential for humans.

maps.label: Cosmic origin (approximate)
maps.caption: The process that made most of each element present when the Solar System formed, read off Fig. 39 of Kobayashi, Karakas & Lugaro (2020) — an approximate transcription of a model, not a measurement.

classes.label: Big Bang
classes.description: Made in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

classes.label: Cosmic rays
classes.description: Split off heavier nuclei by fast cosmic-ray particles.

classes.label: Dying low-mass stars
classes.description: Made in asymptotic-giant-branch stars and blown off in their winds.

classes.label: Exploding massive stars
classes.description: Made in massive stars and their supernova explosions.

classes.label: Merging neutron stars
classes.description: Made by rapid neutron capture when neutron stars collide.

classes.label: Exploding white dwarfs
classes.description: Made in type Ia supernovae, the explosions of white dwarfs.

classes.label: Two equal shares
classes.description: Two processes made about the same share.

classes.label: Not given
classes.description: Not in the model, or the figure cannot be read for this element.
